afternoon. I call to order this March twenty-third, twenty twenty-five Joint Committee with this Board of Supervisors and School Board meeting. Welcome everyone to the LCPS boardroom. Uh, we are happy to host the joint committee this afternoon. Um, we do not have any public comment this afternoon, so we will jump right in with our reports. Um, so this is item three, co-chairs reports on the board of supervisors and school

board activities. I'll start tonight. Um, good evening, joint committee members and to our families and communities watching at home. Uh, this has been an exciting and inspiring few weeks across Loudoun County Public Schools, with many moments that highlight the talent, dedication, and heart of our students and staff. I'd like to begin by recognizing the incredible accomplishments of our students. More than three hundred high school students recently participated in the forty-fourth annual Regional Science and Engineering Fair at Tuscarora High

School. These students demonstrated curiosity, creativity, and critical thinking as they tackled real-world challenges through original research. We are especially proud of those who will advance to the international level and represent LCPS on a global stage. We are also cel-- celebrating the power of words at the regional spelling bee, where Belmont Ridge Middle School student, Vikhyaath Thannamala, claimed the championship after

sixteen impressive rounds, correctly spelling the word peccant. Vikhyaath, along with the runner-upUh, Dia Sudhak-hakar will go on to represent Loudoun County at the Scripps National Spelling Bee this spring. And looking f-toward the future, more than six hundred students from across Virginia participated in the CyberSlam 2026 at George Mason University, gaining hands-on experience in cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and digital forensics, fields that are shaping

tomorrow's workplace. Our success as a d- as a division is made possible by our extraordinary-- the extraordinary dedication of our staff. This month, we are proud to recognize Transportation Supervisor Sue Carlson as the Shine Award recipient. Her commitment to ensuring that every student's transportation needs are met with care and precision exemplifies the very best of LCPS. We also celebrate eight educators who have achieved national board

certification, one of the most rigorous and respected professional accomplishments in education, and congratulate Hannah Boggs of Elaine Thompson Elementary, who was selected for the Fulbright Teachers of Global Classrooms Fellowship. Her upcoming international experience will further enrich learning for her students and our division. In addition, more than two hundred and fifty staff members came together for Inspire Loudon, a division-wide professional learning event focused on innovation, collaboration, and

strengthening instructional practice. LCPS continues to strengthen connections between classroom learning and real-world opportunities. Through our recent Career and Technical Education Roundtable, we partnered with more than one hundred business and community leaders to ensure our programs align with the workforce needs and prepare students for success beyond graduation. And we are excited about upcoming opportunities like the Student Environmental Action Showcase, where students will share innovative ideas to

promote sustainability and make a meaningful impact in our community. Before I close, I would also like to recognize our Transportation Department, which was recently featured nationally for its innovation and commitment to serve, logging millions of miles each year to safely bring our students to and from school. In every classroom competition and collaboration, we see what LCPS-- makes LCPS so special: students who are curious and driven, staff who go above and beyond,

and a community that supports them every step of the way. And I would also like to share that I have appointed Dr. Rasheed, Rasheed to serve as co-chair of this committee. Um, thank you. That concludes my report, and I'll pass over the floor to you, Co-Chair Tichrone. Uh, thank you, Co-Chair Chandler. Uh, Co-Chair Glass is unable to be here today, so as Vice Co-Chair on the Board, on the Board of Supervisors side, I am giving the Co-Chair's report.

First, I would like to congratulate you on being elected Chair of the School Board and, by extension, Co-Chair of this committee. Congratulations. I also want to welcome our new committee members, Dr. Rasheed and Dina Griffiths. We look forward to working with you on all, on continued advocacy for our students. Since the Joint Committee last convened in November, the Board of Supervisors has undertaken several actions that I wish to

highlight. Perhaps most importantly, the board is in the process of concluding our budget, which is slated to be approved at our meeting on Tuesday, April seventh. We undertook several work sessions for the fiscal year twenty twenty-seven budget and kept the real estate property tax rate of eighty and a half cents per hundred dollars in assessed value and successfully lowered the vehicle tax rate by fifteen

cents to two ninety-four per hundred dollars in assessed value. Even with the tax reduction, we can provide several new positions to serve our residents and main-maintain the school board's full budget request. The Board of Supervisors did not fund a request from the sheriff's office to provide school resource officers in all elementary schools. However, the board did fund five additional school resource officers and a sergeant to serve as

floating SROs that be- can be used to backfill and cover vacancies at the middle and high schools. Also related in the budget, as part of the Board of Supervisors' fund balance allocations in January, the board used seventeen and a half million dollars to replenish the Loudoun County Public School Health Self-Insurance Fund and to replace several items at various schools. Two of the items on our committee's work plan the Board of

Supervi-Supervisors has recently acted on include safe passages to school-school's item. The board has begun reviewing the Loudoun's countywide transportation plan. This multi-year update on the plan will review several aspects of our transportation infrastructure that extend beyond vehicles, such as bicycle infrastructure, pedestrian safety, and other alternative modes of transportation. The Board of Supervisors' Transportation and Land

U-Use Committee has also been exploring using county-owned land for attainable housing opportunities. The committee recently had a presentation on an inventory of county land from our Department of Housing and Community Development. On our work plan remains the attainable housing on school property-- i-- on school properties, which will likely be presented in June. I look forward to that discussion. The county also continues to advocate

before the State Corporation Commission on undergrounding power lines around Rock Ridge High School and Rosa Lee Carter as part of Dominion's Golden to Mars power line project. The State Corporation Commission is currently reviewing testimony provided earlier this year. If undergrounding routes are not approved, our respective boards may need to work together to identify the best rou-- be-best above-ground route for the community.Finally, I am pleased to present a

resolution from Virginia, from the Virginia Senate honoring former Broad Run School Board member, Ms. Leslie King. Look at this nice resolution. The resolution was sponsored a few years ago by Senator Jennifer Boysko and was delivered to Supervisor Glass a couple of months ago. After connecting with Ms. King's children, it was the desire of her family to have the resolution housed here at the Loudoun County Public Schools

administration building. Ms. King was elected to the school board in twenty nineteen and served from January twenty twenty until her death in August twenty twenty-one. She is remembered as a kind person who cared deeply for the students and staff in Loudoun County Public Schools. So I'm glad to present that to, to you, Co-chair Vice Chan-- or Co-chair Chamlee. Thank you. Yep. Again, I look forward to working with you and, and, and

build on our shared efforts to serve Loudoun County schools. So this is my report. Thank you. Thank you, Madam Co-chair. Um, with that, we'll move on to our information items. Tonight, our first information item is speed camera enforcement program in school zones. The purpose of this item is for the Leesburg Police Department to provide an update to the joint committee on the status of speed camera enforcement programs run by Lou- Leesburg Police Department near certain Loudoun County Public School campuses in Leesburg.

Um, tonight, this item will be presented, by, Mr. Rob Spano from the Leesburg Police Department, Justin Schumer from the Leesburg Police Department, Mr. Kevin Lewis from Support Services, and Mr. Scott Davies, also from Support Services. Welcome, gentlemen. The floor is yours. Uh, thank you. Yep. Uh, my name's, David Smith. I'm the Deputy Chief of Police for the town of Leesburg Police Department.

So I was gonna primarily, present today and answer any questions that you may have about, our specific program. But, if you wanna go ahead and s- move to the next slide, we can go from there. So, our schools or the school zone speed safety program is b- basically governed by two, two sections of, the Virginia State Code that were put in place here two years ago. So we implemented our program, this last beginning of this, this, this school year, at which of those

two c- state code sections are at the top. And then our, town of Leesburg code, one of the, one of the, the key things as far as in, in, implementing any kind of program is that you have to pass a local ordinance. So town, the, town council had passed our ordinance, which is just specific to, speed zones in, in school zones. So, it do-- The, the laws do allow for other avenues of enforcement, which include, I think it's on your agenda today as far as for stop arm,

on passing of school buses and then also with, red lights. But at this time, right now, the town is, the only thing that we are doing is, the school zone spe- speeding. So I'm ready to move on. So, basically why our program was implemented, it mainly, concerns from the community, m- concerns from, some of our, crossing guards at some of those locations. And then

o- obviously, it's a, it's, it's, a manpower type thing too. So it enables us to do enforcement all the time as far as in the different school zones. So, we picked, we have, we have six cameras currently. We, basically three different school zones. One of the school zones is shared with two schools, which is the, our location there at Harbor Park Middle School, Tolbert and Tol- Tolbert Elementary School, which is one, one zone. It's worked by the same group of crossing guards.

Um, Balls Bluff Elementary School and then Loudoun County High School. Loudoun County High School was a location where we have, had notorious, issues as far as with speeding on Dry Mill Road coming into the town of Leesburg from Loudoun County. Um, so where the s- the speed limit drastically drops off from a very rural area into, right into town. So we've, we've had a lot of issues there. We've kinda picked, we picked our locations based on a number of

different things. One of them, obviously, the traffic volume. Um, we did a number of speed studies in those areas to kinda determine what we were looking at as far as the extent of the speeding problem, the amount of traffic, average vehicles were in there. And then also, we really wanted to get off on a good foot as far as where we picked these locations. So we wanted to pick locations where we knew that we had, pedestrian school traffic. Um, so m- the majority of the, majority of the locations are places where we

have crossing guards, where we're, we're having children cross the road, which is not indicative of all school zones. So we tried to focus on that. So those are some of the main reasons of why we picked where we picked. So, next slide, sir. So we started August twenty-first, which was the, the beginning of, beginning of school this last year. We did a thirty-day warning period, when we, when we went live as far as with the cameras.

Um, that went to September twenty-first, and then in that time that we issued, almost thirteen hundred warnings as far as for speeding on those, six cameras, in, in that, one-month period. Move on. So this will kinda give you an idea of what we've done as far as since. Um, the, obviously the month, self-explanatory of, of when we run the cameras. The, the, the data in March is only

was kinda limited as far as the submission of this presentation. Uh, the number in par- parentheses there by the month is the actual number of school days. I know, like this winter, we had some, you know, I think we had school closed for one week at one point. So, anytime that there was a two-hour delay, things of those nature that certainly, threw off some of the, you know, targeted enforcement kinda things that we would kinda coordinate with.Um, so as you could see, September, 134

citations, and that was, only based on seven days. October, which really was the, the first month of it going live and we're actually issuing citations, obviously our highest number, nineteen school days, and we issued seven hundred and fifty violations in that time. Um, and then shortly thereafter, it starts kinda tapering off. Um, and then, with the next slide, you'll kinda see that, and I'll kinda speak a little bit more towards what, what, what we've seen.

The, the, the first number there, obviously that's our twelve hundred, almost thirteen hundred warnings that occurred as far as in September. And then you see a sharp drop-off to September, which is really more reflective of the seven school days that we actually had in September. And then starting in October, we've seen pretty much a steady decrease through current day, but it's fairly leveled off where we're, you know, in that four or five hundred violations, you know, per month kinda period, which is pretty indicative of every, every...

From, from my research when we started talking about implementing and putting a program as far as in the town, is pretty-- The-- Everybody that I talked to across the commonwealth was, for the most part, you're gonna see about a fifty percent decrease from year one to year two, from startup time as far as in, in, in violations, that are, that are occurring. So I'm, I'm ready for the next one. So this is basically kind of an

overview of, of, of how the, how the camera actually works as far as on that graphic. Um, our cameras are positioned on the outside of the school zones, facing into the school zones. Um, it's very intentional. Um, it is basically to capture the actual school zone warning lights. So our cameras capture not only still images, they capture video as well. So the point on having them on the outside is there's

unquestionably, you can go back and watch the violation, and you can see that the lights are actually functioning, and, they're working as far as when the violator enters into the zone. So that was a primary reason for that. Um, the law changed this last year about that, that it kinda requires that or puts it, makes a requirement as far as on the municipalities enforcing it to be able to show that the, the lights were actually in, in, in use or were working then.

So having our cameras on the outside, there's clear video evidence, so when the violator or when the, the, the law enforcement officer is reviewing can actually watch the video, and you can see that the lights are indeed working. Um, it also takes two still images, which you'll see reflected there with the two red cars there. It's actually the same car. Um, we call it, you know, shot... It's like basically shot one and shot two. And what it does is it's, it's, it's a, it's used as a kind of a

verification as far as for the speed because the camera work captures those images at predetermined distances. And if we know the distance, and we know the, and we, f-from where the camera is or where it took it, it can verify the radar speed just to make sure it's accurate because we know how fast the, the, the, the, the, the car is able to move in between the two locations. So it's just kind of a double-check. Um, our system is a radar system. There are systems out there as far as

that use laser. Um, we found and we did the research, and we like the, the technology as far as with the radar above that. So that's how we ended up with, with, with what we have. Um, and those are our three, three locations. But basically, the way it works is when a, when a violation is captured, we contract the, the vendor that we use. The c-company's name is Verra Mobility that we're contracting with. So when our, when our violations come in, the first place that

reviews them is actually the vendor. Um, their, the, the location where ours are, first reviewed is in Baltimore. They run a, a location there where, operators t-basically review our violations, and they're looking for license plate verification. They're making sure that the, you know, the li- the license plate matches the vehicle as far as what it's, what it's, what it's showing and as far as in the images or in the video.

Um, they're, you know, making sure there's like no glares, everything is re- everything is readable as far as on the violation. And then they're operating, they're begi- making decisions on what we call, business rules that we set up. So, you know, if, if a, if a fire truck with its lights on were to enter our school zone and pass the camera, it's gonna automatically gonna be kicked out by the vendor before we ever see it. Um, so we have different rules, for different situations

that come up. Maybe it's a police escort with a funeral. Maybe it's, you know, it, it, different situations like that. Um, and then once they do the first review, it'll come to the police department, electronically, and then, we have a staff member who reviews all those violations, and they double-check everything that is checked initially, as far as from, from our, from our vendor. And then if we find everything in line, you know, we're

reviewing the video evidence, we're reviewing the photographic evidence, we're matching that vehicle with that license plate, then we're communicating that information. We're endorsing that violation. It's going back to our vendor, and then our vendor is sending out the citation or if you-- the summons, the correct term as far as that time. But that's basically how the, the review process works on that. I'm ready. Um, this is what one of our cameras look li- look, looks like. Um, they're calibrated twice daily.

They do self internal checks. Um, they actually also, if for some reason, if there's a problem detected with one of the cameras, it shuts down. Um, our vendor's really good in the sense that if we have a problem with our camera, they're, they're, they're out within twenty-four hours, to come fix it, repair, get it back online, whatever the issue may be as far as with the camera. Um, like I said, it's still images, and it's, and it's also on video. And then also, they come out, and they take care of

the calibration of what we need as far as for court, for court purposes as far as when it comes to prosecution if a violation were to come contested later on.Um, these are our locations where we have them. Uh, Loudoun County High School, we run a camera on Dry Mill Road. It's one I referenced earlier. We run another camera on the other side of the school on Catoctin Circle, actually where the W&D crosses Catoctin Circle. Um, it's high pedestrian traffic right in that area.

Uh, Balls Bluff Elementary School, kind of a notorious location for speed with constant communication with a crossing guard, at that location. Um, and, she's definitely very thankful as far as of, of the cameras there in that location. I've li-- I've had lots of conversations there. Um, and then, our, our third location there is Harbor Park Middle School and Tolbert Elementary School. It's a f-four-lane road. Um, it's two schools right s-next to one another.

So I thought it was a good opportunity where we could cover two schools with, with two cameras, where normally we'd just be able to cover one school with two cameras. So those are our six cameras in total. Um, those are our enforcement times. Um, basically, it's a, it's an hour per day per school. It's, you know, half an hour in the morning and a half an hour as far as that afternoon, dismissal. So it's all based around arrival and dismissal time and just the times that obviously the lights are active.

Um, the law does require, like, very conspicuous signage. Um, we'll take an opportunity just to say, I've worked very closely with Elizabeth Kratz here as far as with the schools. Um, as far as in surveying all our school locations and our zones, the very specific signs that need to be up, she was very instrumental in getting all those signs put up. I think her and I actually, when we-- her and I put that sign

up ourselves, and I remember it was August, and it was very hot when we put that sign up, so I thought it was very fitting to put that photo in there. Um, but we do have to have the, the s-the sign there on top of the pole, the school zone, speed photo enforced. That is one that's very specific to the law that, needs to a-advise motorists that that is what is occurring at that location. Move on. Um, like I, I explained, our cameras are only running at the time when the school zone lights are flashing.

Um, that, you know, it's very-- that's, that's basically it. The, the law is very specific to where the cameras can only be used for enforcement as far as for that. Can't use them for surveillance. We can't use them for any other kind of data collection purposes. Very specific laws about as far as data retention as far as on these things. Um, but yeah, that, that's it on that, sir. Um, so we do get, like I said, we-- there's a couple different levels of,

review as far as on the violations. Um, they get rejected for, a number of different, situations, one of which weather-related school closures or delays. So we're in constant communication. We obviously monitor what s-schools are doing, when it comes to, you know, school closures, holidays. All the holidays are loaded into the, loaded into the system ahead of time. As soon as the, those are made public, that w-the-- those are

automatically taken out for any kind of holidays. Uh, weather-related, we always have to stay on top of that, and we're in communication with the vendor. Um, we get violations that'll kick, get kicked out for sun glare. As we obviously know, the sun's constantly moving. We're talking, you know, usually in the morning, as the sun's coming up, different times of the day there or different, um... So we, you know, sometimes that'll have a tendency to, if we don't get a good image of the license plate or someone have an obscured license plate, a lot of times a violation will be kicked out for that.

Um, same thing, a dirty license plate, glare. Um, and then also, but, one of, one of the things that we've recently noticed we didn't really until we started doing this was that we had a couple violations where literally the lights are coming on almost as the vi-as the violator is passing the sign. Um, so the camera can't quite, um... So we've had a couple of them as, that we've just, you know, gotten rid of as we've just, you know, like I said, we're watching the video.

We can tell momentarily. It's like as the people are approaching, the sign is not on. As soon as they pass the sign, it's on, and then they're getting, they're getting captured there on video. So, some of the reasons that some of them are kicked out. But like I said, there's a, there's, there's a couple levels or a couple different times that they're all reviewed. Um, and, so that's basically the way that works. You can move on. Um, I mentioned earlier sort of privacy and data retention. Um, law is very specific about what we can use the cameras

for. We only use the cameras, you know, in, in accordance with the law, which is strictly just for the speeding. Um, like I said, we don't use them for any kind of surveillance video or any of that, any-anything like that. Um, you know, the data is, as soon as the violation is dismissed, within two days, it's, it's purged of the system. Um, and then, once it's paid, it's gone within sixty days. So we don't have any way of going back to, to, to query the system to know, you know, who's received

violations or anything. That's just sort of the interest of privacy and, and, and getting rid of the data. Um, so this is always a question that comes up is, is what if I wasn't driving my vehicle, or someone else was driving my vehicle? So there's a couple different avenues as far as with that, one of which obviously the person can contest it, come to court. Um, they can testify in court to basically the fact that they weren't, they weren't, driving the vehicle.

Another way is they can submit an affidavit. Actually, we'll go through our vendor. It can e-either go through the vendor or go through the court system. Um, through basically it's called a transfer of liability. So you're basically transferring the liability of the hundred dollar fine. All our violations are a hundred dollars, per our ordinance. Um, and, you can transfer it to somebody else. You just need to p-provide that person's, you know, basically

information, so we can forward the summons essentially, to them.Um, so it's just our QR code as far as to give you more, we're being very transparent as far as our other program. Um, I know we met here with the superintendent, before we started the program just to, just to talk a little bit about it and, this will kind of frequently a-ask questions. That'll be a link to our website. Um, but, you know,

purpose, obviously, en-encourage safe driving behavior, slow people down in our school zones. We've definitely seen it's had a positive impact as far as on our school zones. I feel not only just during the school times, I know myself as a motorist, even off duty, when anytime that I'm seeing these signs where there's cameras in use, I think we're overall, we're overall seeing a reduction in speed. Whether the lights on the-- are, are on the school zone or not, people are paying attention. C- it causes people to pay attention. It's having a positive effect

as far as in our community. So it's, it's been very positive for us. Um, like I said, we just in the infancy of it, we just started, you know, with our, with our three, three schools or really four schools or six cameras. Um, and then we're already looking at, expanding that to some additional, school zones, and we're just kinda trying to prio-prio-prioritize those basically by the, the, the pedestrian traffic, because there are some school zones where,

quite frankly, children are not crossing the road. I mean, sure there's, you know, vehicle or traffic, you want people slowing down in those areas in general, but our priority has been the locations where the children are actually crossing the roads as far as the slow motors.
